examples.problem_statement: Find (a) log 2.864³, (b) log √2.864.

solution.operation: Recall the power rule for logarithms
solution.description: Before touching the numbers, recall the rule that a power inside a logarithm can be brought out in front as a multiplier. Both parts of this problem are powers of 2.864, so this single rule handles them both.
The problem supplies the logarithm of 2.864 as 0.4570, read from a log table. Everything that follows is arithmetic on this one value.

solution.operation: Apply the power rule to part (a): $\log(2.864^3)$
solution.description: Apply the power rule to part (a) with base value 2.864 and exponent 3, so the logarithm of the cube becomes 3 times the logarithm of 2.864.

solution.operation: Substitute the known value of $\log 2.864$ into part (a)
solution.description: Replace the logarithm of 2.864 by its tabled value 0.4570, which turns the expression into a plain multiplication.
Multiplying 3 by 0.4570 gives 1.3710, the logarithm of 2.864 cubed.

solution.operation: Apply the power rule to part (b): $\log \sqrt{2.864}$
solution.description: For part (b), rewrite the square root as the one-half power first, then apply the same power rule to bring one-half out in front of the logarithm.

solution.operation: Substitute the known value of $\log 2.864$ into part (b)
solution.description: Substitute the tabled value 0.4570 again, this time to be halved rather than tripled.
Half of 0.4570 is 0.2285, which is the logarithm of the square root of 2.864.

examples.problem_statement: Find the number whose log is 1.4232.

solution.description: This problem runs the previous idea backwards: the logarithm is known and the number is wanted. Entering 1.4232 and pressing the ten-to-the-x key raises 10 to that power, which undoes the common logarithm.
The calculator returns 26.50 after rounding to two decimal places, so 26.50 is the number whose common logarithm is 1.4232.
In part (a) the unknown sits in the exponent, so take the logarithm of both sides. The power rule brings x down in front, leaving x times log 1.06 equal to log 3.
Divide both sides by log 1.06 to isolate x. Using the tabled values 0.4771 and 0.0253 gives x equal to 18.86.
Part (b) has unknowns in two exponents, so again take logarithms of both sides. The exponent 2x+5 multiplies log 12 on the left, and on the right the product becomes log 55 plus 3x times log 7.
Collect every term containing x on the left and every constant term on the right, so that x can be factored out of one side.
Factor out x and divide by its coefficient. Both the numerator and the denominator come out negative, and the quotient gives x equal to 9.700.
Part (c) is handled the same way: take logarithms of both sides so that the exponent x on the left and the exponent x minus 1 on the right each move in front of their logarithm.
Expand the right side and gather the x terms on the left, which leaves minus log 12.6 alone on the right; dividing then expresses x as a single fraction.
Evaluating that fraction with log 41.2 equal to 1.6150 and log 12.6 equal to 1.1004 gives x approximately -2.138. A negative value is reasonable here, since 41.2 grows much faster than 12.6.

examples.problem_statement: Sketch the graphs of (a) $y = x^{3/2}$, (b) $y = -x^{-3/2}$.

solution.description: Start by asking where each function is defined at all. The exponent 3/2 hides a square root, so the first function needs x at least 0; the second also puts x in a denominator, so it needs x strictly greater than 0.

Build a short table of convenient points. For the first curve, x equal to 0, 1, 4 and 9 give y equal to 0, 1, 8 and 27; for the second, x equal to 1, 4, 9 and the fractions 1/4 and 1/9 give y equal to -1, -1/8, -1/27, -8 and -27.

solution.result: \begin{aligned}y = x^{3/2} \\ x \to \infty \\ y \to \infty \\ x \to 0^+ \\ y \to 0 \\ y = -x^{-3/2} \\ x \to \infty \\ y \to 0^- \\ x \to 0^+ \\ y \to -\infty\end{aligned}
solution.description: Check the two ends of the domain before drawing anything. The first function grows without bound as x grows and returns to 0 at the origin; the second creeps up toward 0 from below as x grows and falls without bound as x approaches 0 from the right, so the y-axis is a vertical asymptote.
Mark the tabulated pairs on the coordinate plane: (0,0), (1,1), (4,8) and (9,27) for the first curve, and (1,-1), (4,-0.125), (9,-0.037), (0.25,-8) and (0.111,-27) for the second.

Join the plotted points with a smooth curve that agrees with the end behaviour already found. The first rises from the origin, gently at first and then steeply; the second stays below the x-axis, hugging the y-axis on the left and flattening toward the x-axis on the right.

Read the finished sketches back against the analysis as a check. The first curve should be continuous and increasing for every x at least 0, and the second should be negative everywhere, shrinking in size as x grows and asymptotic to both axes.

concept.technique_name: Finding Polynomial Roots by Synthetic Division

examples.problem_statement: Find the roots of the polynomial using synthetic division and factoring.

solution.description: Write the quartic down so its coefficients 1, 4, -10, -28 and -15 are in front of you; these are the numbers every synthetic division will use.

solution.operation: Use Rational Root Theorem to test possible roots
solution.description: By the Rational Root Theorem any rational root is a factor of the constant term -15 divided by a factor of the leading coefficient 1, which cuts the candidates down to plus or minus 1, 3, 5 and 15.
Try the candidate 3 by synthetic division: bring down the 1, then multiply by 3 and add, column by column. The final entry is 0, so 3 really is a root and x - 3 divides the quartic.
The remaining entries of the bottom row, 1, 7, 11 and 5, are the coefficients of the depressed cubic, so the quartic factors as x - 3 times that cubic.

solution.operation: Test x = -1 on the cubic factor
solution.description: Repeat the division on the cubic, this time with the candidate -1. The remainder is 0 again, so -1 is a root and x + 1 is a factor.
The bottom row 1, 6 and 5 leaves the quadratic x squared plus 6x plus 5, which is now small enough to factor by inspection.
Two numbers with product 5 and sum 6 are 1 and 5, so the quadratic splits into (x + 1)(x + 5) and shows that -1 turns up as a root a second time.
Collect the roots from every factor found: 3 from the first division, -1 from the second, and -1 and -5 from the quadratic, so -1 is a double root.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Note that the roots here are numerically small numbers; that is, 3 is a root but 30 is not, -1 is a root but -15 is not.'}
{'point': 'Hereafter we shall not list integers which are large numerically or fractions with large numerator or denominator among the possible roots.'}
common_mistakes: Stopping after the second division and reporting only three roots; the factor x + 1 appears twice, so -1 is a double root.
Treating the last entry of a synthetic division row as part of the quotient instead of as the remainder, which shifts every coefficient of the depressed polynomial.
Getting the sign backwards: a remainder of 0 for the candidate 3 means x - 3 is a factor, not x + 3.
repair_note: Descriptions were terse label-like fragments rather than instruction; rewrote all eight to explain the mechanics of each synthetic division and why the candidate was chosen. Arithmetic verified as internally consistent (both divisions leave remainder 0 and the quadratic factors as stated). technique_name 'polynomial' named an object, not a method, so corrected to the method the steps use. Scaffold number_line -> grid_construction: the steps build synthetic-division tableaux, not positions on a line.

examples.problem_statement:
Solve, using matrices, the system
\[
\begin{cases}
2x - 3y + 2z = 14 \\
4x + 4y - 3z = 6 \\
3x + 2y - 3z = -2
\end{cases}
\]

solution.description: Convert the system of equations into an augmented matrix for row reduction.
Make the leading coefficient of the first row 1 by dividing the first row by 2.
Eliminate the first column below the pivot by subtracting multiples of R1 from R2 and R3.
Make the leading coefficient of the second row 1 by dividing R2 by 10.
Eliminate the second column below the pivot by subtracting (13/2) times R2 from R3.
Make the leading coefficient of the third row 1 by multiplying R3 by -20.
From the third row, we directly get z = 5.
Substitute z = 5 into the second row equation to solve for y.
Substitute y and z into the first row equation to solve for x.

examples.answer: The system has a unique solution: x = 2, y = 0, z = 5

key_reminders: {'point': 'Three essential row operations are highlighted: (a) scaling a row to get 1, (b) adding scaled rows to get 0, (c) swapping rows when needed.'}
{'point': "The approach is structured in 'attacks' — one per column — to systematically reduce the matrix."}
{'point': 'Emphasis on planning each phase to achieve prescribed forms (triangular, then diagonal, then identity).'}
repair_note: Not a narration defect. Contradictory arithmetic between steps. Step 5 applies R3 = R3 - (13/2)R2 to the rows produced in steps 3 and 4, which yields -29/20 and -87/10, but the step 5 result records -1/20 and -1/4. The error propagates: step 6 then reports z = 5, steps 8 and 9 derive y = 13/10 and x = 79/20, and the answer field instead states x = 2, y = 0, z = 5, which fails the second original equation (8 + 0 - 15 = -7, not 6). Three mutually inconsistent numeric claims sit in the unmodifiable layer.

examples.problem_statement: 41.2(a) Show that −1 and 2 are roots of x⁴ − 9x² + 4x + 12 = 0.

solution.description: Test -1 by substituting it for x in the quartic. The four terms give 1, -9, -4 and 12, which cancel to 0, so -1 is a root.
Do the same with 2: the terms 16, -36, 8 and 12 also sum to 0, so 2 is a root as well.

Knowing -1 is a root, divide the quartic by x + 1 with synthetic division, remembering the 0 coefficient for the missing x cubed term. The final 0 confirms the root, and the row 1, -1, -8, 12 gives the cubic quotient.

solution.operation: Synthetic division with root 2 on quotient
solution.description: Divide that cubic by x - 2 the same way, using the other known root. The remainder is again 0, leaving the quadratic coefficients 1, 1 and -6.
Factor x squared plus x minus 6 by finding two numbers with product -6 and sum 1, namely 3 and -2.
Assemble every factor found: x + 1 from the first division, x - 2 from the second, and x + 3 and x - 2 from the quadratic, so the factor x - 2 occurs twice.
Read the roots straight off the factors: -3, -1, and 2, which counts twice because its factor appears twice.

examples.problem_statement: 41.2(b) Show that the equation in (a) has at least two other roots by finding them.

solution.operation: Apply Factor Theorem: since x+1 is a factor, divide original polynomial by (x+1) to get cubic: x³ − x² − 8x + 12.
solution.description: Part (b) picks up where (a) left off. Since -1 was shown to be a root, the Factor Theorem says x + 1 divides the quartic, and dividing it out leaves the cubic x cubed minus x squared minus 8x plus 12.

solution.operation: Use synthetic division with root 2 on cubic x³ − x² − 8x + 12.
solution.description: Use the other root already known, 2, to divide the cubic by synthetic division, which reduces the problem to a quadratic.

solution.operation: Factor the resulting quadratic: x² + x − 6 = (x + 3)(x − 2).
solution.description: Factor the remaining quadratic x squared plus x minus 6 into (x + 3)(x - 2); this is where the two extra roots asked for come from.
Writing the quartic as the product of all four linear factors displays the complete root list at a glance, with x - 2 appearing twice.

examples.answer: Roots are −1, 2, −3, 2 (with 2 being a double root).

examples.problem_statement: 41.5: Solve 2x⁴ − x³ − 11x² + 4x + 12 = 0 using Rational Root Theorem.

solution.description: Here the leading coefficient is 2, so the candidate roots are factors of 12 over factors of 2, which includes halves as well as whole numbers.

solution.operation: Test x=2 via synthetic division: coefficients [2, -1, -11, 4, 12] → quotient 2x³ + 3x² − 5x − 6.
solution.description: Test 2 by synthetic division on the coefficients 2, -1, -11, 4 and 12. The remainder is 0, so 2 is a root and the quotient is the cubic 2x cubed plus 3x squared minus 5x minus 6.

solution.operation: Test x=−1 on quotient: synthetic division yields 2x² + x − 6.
solution.description: Test -1 on that cubic in the same way. It divides evenly, leaving the quadratic 2x squared plus x minus 6.
Factor the quadratic into (2x - 3)(x + 2), which supplies the last two roots, 3/2 and -2.

key_reminders: {'point': 'NOTE: Since x − 2 appears twice among the factors of f(x), 2 appears twice among the roots of f(x) = 0 and is a double root of the equation.'}
{'point': 'Cross-reference to Chapter 43 for Factor Theorem.'}
common_mistakes: Omitting the 0 coefficient for the missing x cubed term when setting up the synthetic division of the quartic; every entry after it then comes out wrong.
Counting 2 only once. The factor x - 2 comes out of two separate steps, so 2 is a double root.
Confusing a root with the sign inside its factor: the root 2 gives the factor x - 2, while the root -3 gives x + 3.

concept.technique_name: Rational Root Theorem with Synthetic Division

solution.operation: List possible rational roots using Rational Root Theorem
solution.result: \pm\frac{\text{factors of constant term}}{\text{factors of leading coefficient}} = \pm1, \pm3, \pm\frac{1}{2}, \pm\frac{3}{2}, \pm\frac{1}{4}, \pm\frac{3}{4}
solution.description: Set up the candidate list before testing anything. With constant term 3 and leading coefficient 4, any rational root is a factor of 3 over a factor of 4.
Try 1 first. The coefficients 4, -3, -4 and 3 add to 0, so 1 is a root and x - 1 is a factor; this shortcut works for any polynomial whose coefficients sum to zero.
Dividing out x - 1 lowers the degree by one and leaves the cubic 4x cubed plus x squared plus x minus 3 to work on.

solution.operation: Test x = 3/4 in the cubic polynomial
solution.description: Test the candidate 3/4 in that cubic. Written over the common denominator 64 the terms are 108, 36, 48 and -192, which cancel exactly, so 3/4 is a root.
Because 3/4 is a root, 4x - 3 is a factor. Dividing the cubic by it leaves the quadratic x squared plus x plus 1.

solution.operation: Solve the quadratic equation x^2 + x + 1 = 0
solution.description: Solve the leftover quadratic with the quadratic formula. Its discriminant is 1 minus 4, which is -3, so the remaining two roots are a complex conjugate pair and no further rational roots exist.
Put the pieces together: the quartic is x - 1 times 4x - 3 times the quadratic x squared plus x plus 1, which cannot be factored further over the real numbers.

examples.answer: The rational roots are x = 1 and x = 3/4. The complete factorization is (x-1)(4x-3)(x^2+1) = 0

solution.description: Every term of this equation contains at least x squared, so pull that common factor out first. It accounts for the root 0 twice over and leaves a quartic to solve.

solution.operation: List possible rational roots of quartic: ±1, ±2, ±1/2, ±1/3, ±2/3, ±1/4, ...
solution.description: For the quartic factor, list the candidates as factors of the constant -2 over factors of the leading coefficient 24, which produces a long list of halves, thirds and quarters.

solution.operation: Test rational roots using synthetic division; find x=1/2 is a root.
solution.description: Work through the candidates with synthetic division until one leaves remainder 0; the value 1/2 does.

solution.operation: Factor out (x - 1/2) and continue factoring the resulting cubic.
solution.description: Divide out x - 1/2 to drop the quartic to a cubic, then keep applying the same test-and-divide process to that cubic.
The reduction ends at the quadratic 6x squared plus x minus 2, which factors directly into (2x - 1)(3x + 2), giving 1/2 once more together with -2/3.

solution.operation: Note alternating signs → rational roots, if any, are positive.
solution.description: Look at the signs before testing anything: they alternate all the way down, so no negative value can make the left side zero. That halves the work.
List only the positive candidates, factors of the constant 25 over factors of the leading coefficient 4, so 1, 5, 1/2, 5/2, 1/4 and so on.

solution.operation: Test x=5/2 using synthetic division; confirm it is a root.
solution.description: Synthetic division with 5/2 leaves remainder 0, which confirms 5/2 as a root of the quintic.

solution.operation: Repeat synthetic division with x=5/2 on quotient to find multiplicity 2.
solution.description: Run the same division again on the quotient. It divides evenly a second time, so 5/2 is a root of multiplicity 2 rather than a simple root.

solution.operation: Factor remaining cubic: x^3 - 3x^2 + 2x - 1; test x=1 → not a root.
solution.description: What is left is the cubic x cubed minus 3x squared plus 2x minus 1. Testing 1 in it gives 1 - 3 + 2 - 1, which is -1 rather than 0, so 1 is not a root and this cubic yields no further rational roots.

examples.answer: The rational roots are 5/2, 5/2. The cubic has one irrational real root.

solution.description: With constant term 1 and leading coefficient 6, the candidate list is short: plus or minus 1, 1/2, 1/3 and 1/6.

solution.operation: Test each possible root using substitution or synthetic division.
solution.description: Check each candidate in turn, by substitution or by synthetic division; the list is small enough to exhaust completely.

solution.operation: None of the candidates satisfy the equation.
solution.description: Not one candidate gives zero, so by the Rational Root Theorem this equation has no rational root at all. Whatever real roots it has must be irrational.

examples.answer: The equation has no rational roots.

examples.problem_statement: Find the equation each of whose roots is 4 less than the roots of $x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x - 12 = 0$.

solution.description: Read what is being asked. If r is a root of the given cubic, the new equation must have r - 4 as a root, so calling the new variable y and setting y equal to r - 4 sets up the substitution.

solution.operation: Substitute x = y + 4 into the original equation
solution.description: Since y equals x - 4, we have x equal to y + 4. Putting y + 4 wherever x appears rewrites the equation in y, and its roots are automatically 4 less than the original ones.
Expand the cubed term by the binomial theorem, which gives y cubed plus 12y squared plus 48y plus 64.
Expand the squared term and multiply the result by 3, giving 3y squared plus 24y plus 48.
Distribute the -4 across y + 4 to get -4y minus 16.
Put the three expanded pieces back into the equation, keeping the constant -12 carried over from the original cubic.
Group the terms by degree so that the coefficients of each power of y can be added in one place.
Add within each group: 12 plus 3 gives 15, 48 plus 24 minus 4 gives 68, and 64 plus 48 minus 16 minus 12 gives 84, which produces the transformed cubic.

key_reminders: {'point': 'On the left the successive remainders have been found and circled.'}
{'point': 'The resulting equation is y³ + 15y² + 68y + 84 = 0.'}
{'point': 'The given equation has roots x = 2, -2 - 3; on the right, it is shown that 2 - 4 = -2, -2 - 4 = -6, -3 - 4 = -7 are roots of the newly formed equation.'}
common_mistakes: Substituting x equal to y - 4 instead of y + 4; to lower every root by 4 you replace x with y + 4.
Dropping the constant -12 of the original cubic when the terms are collected, which spoils the final constant.
Expanding the cube of y + 4 as y cubed plus 64 and losing the two middle binomial terms.
